lessons.title: Salvē! How Latin sounds
lessons.summary: Read Latin aloud the way the Romans did, and say hello.
objectives: Pronounce Latin letters the classical way
Tell long vowels from short ones
Greet one person, or a group

steps.title: Latin is read as it is written
body: Latin spelling is honest. Every letter is pronounced, and each letter always makes the same sound. Learn the sounds once and you can read any word aloud.
Most letters sound as they do in English. A few are different, and they are worth learning now:

rows.label: r
cells: rolled, as in Spanish or Italian

steps.tip: Caesar’s famous boast *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī*, “I came, I saw, I conquered”, sounds like WAY-nee, WEE-dee, WEE-kee.

steps.explain: In classical Latin *c* is always hard, like *k*: KEE-keh-roh.
The Romans said *v* like an English *w*: WEE-tah.

steps.prompt: Which English word rhymes with the first syllable of *Caesar*?
steps.explain: *ae* sounds like the English word *eye*, so *Caesar* is KYE-sar.

steps.title: Long and short vowels
body: Latin vowels come in two lengths, and a long vowel is held about twice as long as a short one. In this course long vowels carry a line over them, called a **macron**: *ā ē ī ō ū*.
Length can change what a word means. *Mālum*, with a long *a*, is an apple; *malum*, with a short one, is something bad.
The Romans did not write macrons, and the AP exam does not print them. But learning words with them makes pronunciation easier now, and poetry much easier later.

steps.explain: The macron marks the *ā* as long. *Mālum* is an apple; *malum*, with a short *a*, is a bad thing.

steps.title: Hello and goodbye
body: Latin greets one person and a group differently. To one person, say *salvē*; to more than one, *salvēte*. Goodbye works the same way: *valē* to one person, *valēte* to several.
*Salvē* means “be well” and *valē* “be strong”. The *-te* on the end is how Latin speaks to more than one person at a time, and you will see it again.

steps.prompt: You walk into a room full of friends. You say:
steps.explain: *Salvēte* greets more than one person. *Salvē* is for one, and *valēte* means goodbye.

steps.prompt: Leaving your teacher at the end of a lesson, you say:
steps.explain: One person, and you are leaving: *valē*.

steps.title: Two small words
body: *Et* means “and”. *Nōn* means “not”, and it usually comes just before the word it denies.

steps.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
Type the Latin for “goodbye”, said to a group.
answers: valēte
steps.explain: *Valēte*: *valē* with *-te* for more than one person.

steps.prompt: Which word starts with a *y* sound?
steps.explain: At the start of a word and before another vowel, *i* is a consonant like English *y*: *iam* is “yahm”. In *īra* and *ita* it is a vowel.

lessons.title: Est: saying who someone is
lessons.summary: “Julia is a girl”, “Marcus is a sailor”, and why Latin needs no “a” or “the”.
objectives: Use *est*, “is”, and *sunt*, “are”
Translate without Latin’s missing “a” and “the”
Know the gender of nouns ending in *-a*

steps.title: No “a”, no “the”
body: Latin has no words for “a” or “the”. *Puella* means “a girl” or “the girl”; English needs one of them, so you add whichever sounds right.
*Est* means “is”. Latin likes to put the verb last, so “Julia is a girl” comes out as *Iūlia puella est*.

answers: Julia is a girl.
Julia is the girl.
Marcus is a farmer.
Marcus is the farmer.

steps.explain: *Poēta* is “poet” and *est* is “is”. English adds the “a”.

steps.title: Masculine and feminine
body: Every Latin noun has a gender: masculine, feminine or neuter. Nouns ending in *-a*, like *puella* and *fēmina*, are nearly all feminine.
A few are masculine because of who they name. *Nauta*, *agricola* and *poēta* were men’s work in the Roman world, so they are masculine even though they look like *puella*.
steps.tip: Gender is a grammar label, not a claim about the world. It matters because adjectives have to match it, as you will see in Unit 3.

steps.explain: It ends in *-a* like a feminine noun, but sailors were men, so *nauta* is masculine.

steps.title: “Are”: sunt
body: For more than one person, “are” is *sunt*, and the nouns change too: *puella*, “girl”, becomes *puellae*, “girls”. Unit 2 covers this properly.

steps.explain: Two people, Marcus and Quintus, so “are”: *sunt*.

steps.source: Iūlia fēmina est.
Marcus is a poet.
steps.explain: Latin usually puts the verb last, but every order of these three words is good Latin.

answers: est
steps.explain: *Est*, as in *Iūlia puella est*.

answers: Julia is not a sailor.
Julia isn't a sailor.
steps.explain: *Nōn* sits just before the word it denies, here *est*.

options: Marcus is a poet, and so is Julia.
Marcus and Julia are not poets.
steps.explain: *Poētae* is the plural, “poets”, and *sunt* is “are”.

lessons.title: Sum: I am, you are
lessons.summary: The whole verb “to be”, and the six endings that tell you who.
objectives: Say “I am”, “you are”, “we are” and the rest
Know the six personal endings: *-ō/-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*
Understand a verb with no separate subject word

steps.title: The verb “to be”
body: A Latin verb changes its ending to show who is doing something, so it does not need a separate word for “I” or “you”. *Sum* on its own means “I am”.

steps.title: The endings tell you who
body: Look at the last letters. They are the same on almost every Latin verb you will ever meet.
steps.tip: Learn this row by heart: *-ō/-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*. It unlocks every verb in the language.

steps.explain: *-mus* means “we”.
*-tis* is “you” speaking to more than one person.

answers: sunt
steps.explain: *-nt* means “they”: *sunt*.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “you are”, said to one person.
answers: es
steps.explain: Just *es*.

steps.prompt: Match each form to its meaning.

answers: I am a poet.
I am the poet.
I'm a poet.
steps.explain: No word for “I” is needed: *sum* already means “I am”.

answers: We are sailors.
We're sailors.

steps.explain: *Sed* is “but”, *et* is “and”, *nōn* is “not”.

steps.latin: Fēmina sum, sed poēta nōn sum.
answers: I am a woman, but I am not a poet.
I'm a woman, but I'm not a poet.
I am a woman but not a poet.

steps.source: We are farmers.

steps.explain: *-tis* is “you (all)”, and *puellae* is the plural “girls”.

lessons.title: Why endings matter
lessons.summary: How Latin shows who does what to whom, whatever the word order.
objectives: Find the subject and the object of a sentence
Recognize the subject ending *-a* and the object ending *-am*
See why Latin word order is free

steps.title: Who does what?
body: In English, word order carries the meaning. “The girl loves the sailor” and “The sailor loves the girl” use the same words in a different order, and say different things.
Latin shows the same thing with endings. The **subject**, who does the action, and the **object**, who has it done to them, have different endings. So the words can go in almost any order.

steps.prompt: In “The farmer sees the poet”, which is the object?
steps.explain: The poet is the one being seen, so the poet is the object.

steps.prompt: In “Julia calls Marcus”, which is the subject?
steps.explain: Julia is doing the calling.

steps.title: Two endings, two jobs
body: For nouns like *puella*, the subject ends in *-a* and the object ends in *-am*. These jobs are called **cases**: the subject is in the **nominative** case, the object in the **accusative**.

examples.note: The same meaning as the first: *puella* is still the subject.

steps.explain: *Iūlia* ends in *-a*, the subject ending. *Poētam* ends in *-am*: the poet is the one being seen.
The order changed, but the endings did not: Julia still sees the poet.

steps.prompt: Which sentence means “The sailor loves the girl”?
steps.explain: The sailor is the subject (*nauta*) and the girl the object (*puellam*). The other two both say the girl loves the sailor.

answers: The farmer sees the woman.
The farmer sees a woman.
A farmer sees a woman.
The farmer sees the woman.
The farmer sees a woman.
steps.explain: *Agricola* is still the subject; only the order changed.

steps.prompt: Make *puella* the object: type its accusative.
answers: puellam
steps.explain: Add *-m*: *puellam*.

answers: fēminam
steps.explain: *Fēminam*.

steps.source: Nautam poēta amat.
steps.explain: *Poēta* ends in *-a*, so the poet is the subject, even though it comes second.

steps.source: The woman sees the girl.
steps.explain: The woman is the subject (*fēmina*) and the girl the object (*puellam*), in any order.

lessons.title: One girl, many girls
lessons.summary: Singular and plural, subject and object: *puella, puellae, puellam, puellās*.
objectives: Make first-declension nouns plural
Tell a plural subject from a plural object
Match the verb to its subject: *-t* for one, *-nt* for more

steps.title: Plurals
body: The nouns you know so far all belong to the **first declension**: a family of nouns that share one set of endings. In the plural, the subject ends in *-ae* and the object in *-ās*.

steps.title: The verb agrees
body: A verb’s ending matches its subject: *-t* when the subject is one person or thing, *-nt* when it is more than one.

examples.en: The sailor looks at the islands.

steps.explain: *-ās* is the plural object ending.
*Agricolae* is plural, farmers, so the verb takes *-nt*.

steps.prompt: Type the plural object form of *via*, “roads”.
answers: viās
steps.explain: *Via* becomes *viās*.

steps.prompt: Type the plural subject form of *īnsula*, “islands”.
answers: īnsulae
steps.explain: *Īnsulae*.

answers: The sailors carry water.
The sailors are carrying water.
Sailors carry water.
The poet looks at the islands.
The poet watches the islands.
The poet is looking at the islands.

options: The woman and the girls call.
steps.explain: *Fēmina* is the subject (*-a*, with a singular verb); *puellās* is the object.

steps.source: The girls call the farmer.
Fēminae viās spectant.

lessons.title: Amō: the present tense
lessons.summary: Verbs like *amō*, “I love”, in all six persons.
objectives: Find a verb’s stem from its infinitive
Conjugate a first-conjugation verb in the present tense
Translate the present as “I love” or “I am loving”

steps.title: Two forms to learn every verb by
body: A verb is listed with its first form, “I love”, and its **infinitive**, “to love”: *amō, amāre*. Take *-re* off the infinitive and you have the **stem**, *amā-*.
Verbs whose stem ends in *-ā-* form the **first conjugation**. Add the endings you learned with *sum* to the stem, and you have the present tense.
steps.tip: In *amō* the stem’s *ā* disappears into the *-ō*, and it is short before *-t* and *-nt*. Otherwise the stem stays whole.

steps.title: One Latin present, three English ones
body: *Amō* can mean “I love”, “I am loving” or “I do love”. Choose whichever reads best in English.

steps.explain: Take *-re* off the infinitive: *ambulā-*.

answers: nāvigāmus
steps.explain: *Nāvigā-* plus *-mus*: *nāvigāmus*.

answers: ambulātis
steps.explain: *Ambulā-* plus *-tis*.

answers: laudō
steps.explain: *Laudō*: the stem’s *-ā-* is swallowed by the *-ō*.
*-nt* is “they”.

steps.prompt: Match each form to its meaning.

answers: We walk and sail.
We walk and we sail.
We are walking and sailing.
You praise the poet.
You are praising the poet.
steps.explain: *-s* is “you”, and *poētam* is the object.

answers: The sailors do not fight.
The sailors don't fight.
The sailors are not fighting.

steps.source: I love the island.

steps.explain: The stem’s *ā* is short before *-t*: *portat*.

lessons.title: Of, to, with: the other three cases
lessons.summary: Genitive, dative and ablative, and the whole first declension.
objectives: Decline a first-declension noun in all five cases
Translate the genitive “of”, the dative “to, for”, and the ablative “by, with, from, in”
Use *in* and *cum* with the ablative

steps.title: Five cases
body: Latin nouns have five everyday cases. You know two already. Here is the whole first declension:
steps.tip: The ablative singular *puellā* has a long *ā*; the nominative *puella* has a short one. The macron is often the only way to tell them apart.

steps.title: What each case does
body: The **genitive** means “of”, and shows whose something is. The **dative** means “to” or “for”, and marks the person something is given or told to. The **ablative** means “by, with, from” or “in”, often with a preposition.

examples.en: the farmer’s daughter (the daughter of the farmer)
The poet gives a rose to the girl.

examples.note: An ablative alone can mean “by means of”.

steps.explain: *-ārum* is the genitive plural.

options: It is the object of a verb
steps.explain: *In* meaning “in” or “on” is followed by the ablative.

steps.prompt: Type the genitive plural of *fēmina*, “of the women”.
answers: fēminārum
steps.explain: *Fēminārum*.

steps.prompt: Type the ablative singular of *silva*, as in “in the forest”.
answers: silvā
steps.explain: *Silvā*, with a long *ā*.

steps.prompt: Type the dative plural of *nauta*, “to the sailors”.
answers: nautīs
steps.explain: *Nautīs*, the same form as the ablative plural.

answers: The sailor's daughter carries water.
The daughter of the sailor carries water.
The sailor's daughter is carrying water.
The poet gives roses to the girls.
The poet gives the girls roses.
The poet is giving roses to the girls.
I walk with my daughter.
I walk with the daughter.
I am walking with my daughter.
I walk with a daughter.
steps.explain: Latin often leaves out “my”, “his” and “her” when the meaning is plain.

steps.latin: Agricolae in terrā puellīs aquam dant.
options: The farmers give water to the girls on the land.
The farmer’s girls give water on the land.
The farmers give the land’s water to the girls.
steps.explain: *Agricolae* goes with *dant*, a plural subject; *puellīs* is the dative “to the girls”; *in terrā* is “on the land”.

steps.source: The women walk in the forest.
steps.explain: *In silvā* stays together, since a preposition comes right before its noun; otherwise any order is good Latin. (*In silvam* would be “into the forest”.)

steps.prompt: Match each case to its usual meaning.

lessons.title: Reading: Iūlia et nautae
lessons.summary: A first story, and questions on it.
objectives: Read a short connected story in Latin
Follow the cases through several sentences

steps.title: Iūlia et nautae
steps.intro: Julia, a farmer’s daughter, meets some sailors. Read each line in Latin first, then check yourself against the translation.

lines.la: Iūlia puella est. Iūlia fīlia agricolae est.
lines.en: Julia is a girl. Julia is the farmer’s daughter.

lines.la: Agricola et fīlia in terrā labōrant.
lines.en: The farmer and his daughter work on the land.

lines.la: Nautae ad īnsulam nāvigant.
lines.en: Sailors are sailing to the island.

lines.la: Iūlia nautās spectat et vocat: “Salvēte, nautae!”
lines.en: Julia watches the sailors and calls, “Hello, sailors!”

lines.la: Nautae puellam salūtant.
lines.en: The sailors greet the girl.

lines.la: Ūnus nauta Iūliae rosam dat.
lines.en: One sailor gives Julia a rose.

lines.la: Iūlia rosam amat, sed nautās nōn amat!
lines.en: Julia loves the rose, but she does not love the sailors!

lines.la: Nautae iterum nāvigant. “Valēte, nautae!”
lines.en: The sailors sail on again. “Goodbye, sailors!”

steps.explain: *Fīlia agricolae*: *agricolae* is genitive, “of the farmer”.

steps.prompt: Where do Julia and her father work?
steps.explain: *In terrā*, with the ablative: “on the land”.

steps.prompt: In *Ūnus nauta Iūliae rosam dat*, what case is *Iūliae*?
steps.explain: The rose is given to Julia: dative.

options: She loves the rose and the sailors.
She loves the rose, not the sailors.
She loves the sailors, not the rose.
steps.explain: *Rosam amat, sed nautās nōn amat.*

answers: The sailors greet the girl.
The sailors are greeting the girl.
Sailors greet the girl.

options: She is speaking to more than one sailor
steps.explain: *-te* speaks to more than one person.

units.title: The second declension and adjectives
units.blurb: Nouns like *servus*, *puer* and *bellum*, adjectives that agree, and verbs like *moneō*.

lessons.title: Servus, dominus: the second declension
lessons.summary: A second family of nouns, mostly masculine, ending in *-us*.
objectives: Decline a second-declension noun in *-us*
Tell *servī* “slaves” from *servī* “of the slave” by context
Use first- and second-declension nouns in one sentence

steps.title: A second family
body: The **second declension** is the other big family of nouns. Most of its members end in *-us* and are masculine.
The dictionary gives each noun with its genitive singular: *servus, servī*. The genitive tells you the family: *-ae* for the first declension, *-ī* for the second.
steps.tip: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, and *servus* is one of the commonest words you will read. The course uses the word plainly, as the Romans did.

steps.title: Same endings, different jobs
body: Some endings do two jobs. *Servī* can be the plural subject, “slaves”, or the genitive singular, “of the slave”. The verb and the rest of the sentence decide.

examples.note: *Portant* is plural, so *servī* is the plural subject.

examples.en: The slave’s friend is a sailor.
The master gives water to the slaves.

steps.explain: *-ōs* is the accusative plural of the second declension, like *-ās* in the first.
*Spectat* is singular, so the subject is *fīlius*; *dominī* is genitive, “of the master”. The master’s son watches the horse.

answers: amīcum
steps.explain: *Amīcum*.

steps.prompt: Type the genitive plural of *equus*, “of the horses”.
answers: equōrum
steps.explain: *Equōrum*, matching *puellārum* in the first declension.

answers: The master calls the slave.
The master is calling the slave.
The friends watch the horses.
The friends look at the horses.
Friends watch the horses.
The farmer's son calls his friend.
The farmer's son calls a friend.
The son of the farmer calls his friend.
The farmer's son calls the friend.

steps.source: The friend gives water to the horse.
steps.explain: The horse is the one given to, so dative: *equō*.

steps.prompt: Which ending marks the dative and ablative plural in both declensions you know?
steps.explain: *Puellīs* and *servīs*: *-īs* for both cases, in both declensions.

lessons.title: Puer, ager, bellum
lessons.summary: Second-declension nouns in *-er*, and neuters in *-um*.
objectives: Decline nouns like *puer* and *ager*
Know the neuter rule: nominative and accusative are the same
Recognize a neuter plural in *-a*

steps.title: Nouns in -er
body: A few second-declension nouns end in *-er* in the nominative. After that they take the usual endings. Some keep the *e*, like *puer, puerī*; some drop it, like *ager, agrī*. The genitive in the dictionary entry tells you which.
*Vir, virī*, “man”, belongs here too, with no *-us* at all.

steps.prompt: Type the ablative singular of *ager*, as in “in the field”.
answers: agrō
steps.hint: The genitive is *agrī*: the *e* is gone.
steps.explain: *In agrō*.

answers: puerōs
steps.explain: *Puerōs*: *puer* keeps its *e*.

steps.title: Neuters
body: Latin’s third gender is the **neuter**, “neither”. Second-declension neuters end in *-um* and are declined like *servus*, except for one rule that holds for every neuter noun in the language:
**The nominative and accusative are always the same**, and in the plural both end in *-a*.
steps.tip: A neuter plural in *-a* looks like a first-declension singular. *Dōna* is “gifts”, not one gift; the verb usually shows it.

steps.explain: A neuter plural: nominative or accusative, “gifts”.

steps.prompt: Is *oppidum* the subject or the object here?
steps.explain: *Oppidum* could be either, since it is neuter. But *puerī* is the plural subject that goes with *spectant*, so the town is what they look at.

answers: The boys walk in the field.
The boys are walking in the field.
Boys walk in the field.
The man gives the boy a gift.
The man gives a gift to the boy.
The man gives the gift to the boy.
The man is giving the boy a gift.
We do not love wars.
We don't love wars.
We do not love war.
We don't like wars.

steps.source: The men carry the gifts to the town.
steps.explain: *Ad oppidum*, “to the town”, uses *ad* with the accusative. *Dōna* is the neuter plural object.
Second-declension nouns in *-um* are neuter.

lessons.title: Bonus, bona, bonum: adjectives
lessons.summary: Adjectives take the gender, number and case of their noun.
objectives: Choose the right form of a first- and second-declension adjective
See that an adjective agrees in gender, not in look
Use an adjective on its own as a noun

steps.title: Three forms, one word
body: An adjective is listed with three forms, masculine, feminine and neuter: *bonus, bona, bonum*. It declines like *servus* in the masculine and neuter, and like *puella* in the feminine.
An adjective takes the **gender, number and case** of the noun it describes. That is called **agreement**.
steps.tip: Latin usually puts the adjective after its noun, but adjectives of size and number, like *magnus* and *multī*, often come first.

steps.title: Agreement, not rhyme
body: Agreement is in gender, which is not always the same as matching endings. *Nauta* is masculine, so a good sailor is *nauta bonus*. The endings differ, and that is correct.

steps.explain: *Nauta* is masculine, so *bonus*, even though the endings do not match.
*Puerī* is masculine, plural and nominative, so *multī*. “Many boys are walking in the road.”

answers: bonam
steps.explain: Feminine, singular, accusative: *bonam*.

answers: magna
steps.explain: Neuter plural nominative or accusative: *magna*.

answers: bonōs
steps.explain: *Nautās* is masculine accusative plural, so *bonōs*.

steps.title: Adjectives as nouns
body: An adjective can stand on its own, with the noun understood from its gender: *bonī* “good men, good people”, *multī* “many people”, *multa* “many things”.

examples.en: Good people do not love wars.

answers: The poet is great.
The poet is a great poet.
He is a great poet.
The poet is big.
steps.explain: *Magnus* can be “big” or “great”; with a poet, “great” is the natural choice.

answers: I love the small horse.
I love the little horse.
I love a small horse.
The women are happy.
The women are glad.

steps.source: The bad slaves do not love the good master.
steps.explain: Each adjective sits with its noun: *servī malī*, *dominum bonum*. *Nōn* goes before the verb.

steps.prompt: Match each adjective to its meaning.

lessons.title: Moneō: the second conjugation
lessons.summary: Verbs with *-ē-*: *moneō, habeō, videō, timeō*, and asking a question with *-ne*.
objectives: Conjugate a second-conjugation verb in the present
Tell the first conjugation from the second by the infinitive
Ask a yes-or-no question with *-ne*

steps.title: Stems in -ē-
body: Verbs like *moneō, monēre* belong to the **second conjugation**. Their stem ends in *-ē-*: take *-re* off *monēre* and you have *monē-*.
The endings are the same as for *amō*. The difference is the vowel, and the *-eō* in the first form, which keeps its *e*.
steps.tip: The infinitive tells the families apart: *-āre* is the first conjugation, *-ēre* (with a long *ē*) the second.

steps.explain: *Habēre* ends in *-ēre*.

answers: habent
steps.explain: *Habe-* plus *-nt*.

answers: vidētis
steps.explain: *Vidē-* plus *-tis*.

answers: timeō
steps.explain: *Timeō*: the *e* stays in the second conjugation.

steps.title: Asking a question: -ne
body: To ask a yes-or-no question, add *-ne* to the first word of the sentence, usually the verb. There is no Latin word for “yes”; you answer by repeating the verb.

examples.en: Are you afraid of the horse?

steps.explain: *-ne* turns *habēs*, “you have”, into a question.

answers: The master warns the slaves.
The master is warning the slaves.
The master advises the slaves.
The boys fear the big horse.
The boys are afraid of the big horse.
The boys fear the large horse.
We do not have water.
We don't have water.
We have no water.
We do not have any water.

steps.source: Vidēsne oppidum?

lessons.title: Reading: Mārcus et equus
lessons.summary: A boy, a friend, and a large horse in a field.
objectives: Read a story using both declensions
Follow adjectives to the nouns they describe

steps.title: Mārcus et equus
steps.intro: Marcus and his friend meet a horse. Read each line in Latin first.

lines.la: Mārcus puer Rōmānus est.
lines.en: Marcus is a Roman boy.

lines.la: Mārcus in agrō cum amīcō ambulat.
lines.en: Marcus is walking in a field with his friend.

lines.la: In agrō est equus magnus.
lines.en: In the field there is a big horse.

lines.la: Puerī equum vident, sed equus puerōs nōn videt.

units.title: Prepositions, the ablative, past and future
units.blurb: Where to and where from, what the ablative does on its own, and two new tenses: *was doing* and *will do*.

lessons.title: Where to, where from
lessons.summary: Prepositions with the accusative and with the ablative, and the two meanings of *in*.
objectives: Know which prepositions take the accusative and which the ablative
Tell *in silvam* “into the forest” from *in silvā* “in the forest”
Translate prepositional phrases of place and motion

steps.title: Two kinds of preposition
body: Each Latin preposition takes a particular case after it. Roughly: **motion toward** takes the accusative; **place where** and **motion away** take the ablative.
steps.tip: Before a vowel, use *ab* and *ex*: *ab īnsulā*, *ex oppidō*. Before a consonant, *ā* and *ē* are common: *ā silvā*, *ē terrā*.

steps.title: In: into, or in
body: *In* takes either case, and the case changes the meaning. With the accusative it is motion, “into” or “onto”. With the ablative it is place, “in” or “on”.

examples.en: The boys walk into the forest.
The boys walk in the forest.

steps.explain: *Oppidum* here is accusative, so *in* means motion: “into the town”.
*Ē, ex* “out of” takes the ablative, like every “away from” preposition.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “into the forest”.
answers: in silvam
steps.explain: *In* with the accusative: *in silvam*.

answers: sine aquā
steps.explain: *Sine* takes the ablative: *sine aquā*.

lessons.title: The ablative on its own
lessons.summary: With a sword, with great care, at the first hour: the ablative without a preposition.
objectives: Translate the ablative of means: *gladiō* “with a sword”
Tell means (no preposition) from company (*cum*)
Recognize the ablative of manner and of time when

steps.title: By means of
body: An ablative without any preposition often means the tool or means by which something is done. English says “with” or “by”.

examples.en: The sailor fights with a spear.
The girl washes the horse with water.

steps.title: With a thing, or with a person
body: English uses “with” for both the tool and the company, but Latin does not. The tool is a bare ablative. A person you are with needs *cum*.

examples.en: he fights with a sword (the tool)
he fights with a friend (his companion, or his enemy)

steps.prompt: “The farmer works with his son.” How is “with his son” said?
steps.explain: A person you are with takes *cum*.

steps.prompt: “The boys fight with spears.” How is “with spears” said?
steps.explain: Spears are the means, so a bare ablative: *hastīs*.

steps.title: How, and when
body: The ablative also says **how** something is done, usually with an adjective and often with *cum* tucked in the middle: *magnā cum cūrā*, “with great care”.
And it says **when**: *prīmā hōrā*, “at the first hour”. No preposition is needed.

examples.en: We walk at the first hour.
examples.note: *Prīmus, -a, -um*: first. The Roman day began at sunrise.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “with swords” (as a tool).
answers: gladiīs
steps.explain: A bare ablative plural: *gladiīs*.

answers: The farmer works with great care.
The farmer is working with great care.
The farmer works very carefully.
The sailors fight with spears and swords.
The sailors are fighting with spears and swords.

steps.prompt: What kind of ablative is *prīmā hōrā*?
options: time when: at the first hour
steps.explain: A word for a time in the ablative says when: “at the first hour”.

steps.source: The man fights with a sword.
steps.explain: The sword is the means: *gladiō*, with no *cum*.

lessons.title: Amābam: the imperfect
lessons.summary: What was going on, or used to happen: *-bā-* and *eram*.
objectives: Form the imperfect of the first and second conjugations
Say “I was, you were” with *eram*
Translate the imperfect as “was doing” or “used to do”

steps.title: Was doing
body: The **imperfect** tense describes the past as ongoing: what was happening, or what used to happen again and again. Its sign is *-bā-*, added to the stem, followed by the personal endings (with *-m* for “I”).
steps.tip: *Amābat* can be “he was loving”, “he used to love”, or simply “he loved”, when it describes a state of things. Choose what sounds natural.

steps.title: I was: eram
body: *Sum* is irregular in the imperfect, but simple: *er-* plus *-am, -ās, -at, -āmus, -ātis, -ant*.

steps.explain: *-bā-* marks the imperfect, and *-mus* is “we”.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “they used to live”, from *habitō*.
answers: habitābant
steps.explain: *Habitā-* plus *-bant*.

answers: eram
steps.explain: *Eram*.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “you (one person) were seeing”, from *videō*.

steps.explain: *Vidē-* plus *-bās*.

lessons.title: Amābō: the future
lessons.summary: *Will do*: the future of the first two conjugations, and *erō*.
objectives: Form the future of the first and second conjugations
Say “I will be” with *erō*
Tell *-ba-* (was) from *-bi-* (will)

steps.title: Will do
body: For the first two conjugations, the future adds *-b-* and a short vowel to the stem: *-bō, -bis, -bit, -bimus, -bitis, -bunt*.
steps.tip: A rhyme to keep them apart: *-bō, -bi, -bu* is the future; *-ba* is the past.

steps.title: I will be: erō
body: The future of *sum* is *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt*.

examples.en: Soon you will be a sailor.

steps.explain: *-bunt* is future.
*Vidēbāmus*, with *-ba-*, is imperfect: “we were seeing”. *Vidēbimus* is future.

units.blurb: The largest family of nouns (*rēx*, *nōmen*, *urbs*), the other two conjugations, and how to give an order.

lessons.title: Rēx, rēgis: the third declension
lessons.summary: Nouns whose stem hides in the genitive.
objectives: Find a third-declension noun’s stem from its genitive
Decline consonant-stem nouns, masculine, feminine and neuter
Recognize *-em*, *-ibus* and *-ēs*

steps.title: The stem is in the genitive
body: The **third declension** is the biggest family of Latin nouns, and the nominative singular can end in almost anything: *rēx*, *mīles*, *homō*, *nōmen*.
So the genitive matters more than ever. Take *-is* off the genitive and you have the stem that every other form is built on: *rēgis* → *rēg-*, *mīlitis* → *mīlit-*.
steps.tip: Watch the dative singular *-ī* and the second-declension genitive *-ī*: *rēgī* is “to the king”, *servī* is “of the slave”.

steps.title: Neuters
body: Third-declension neuters follow the rule you know: nominative and accusative alike, plural in *-a*.

steps.prompt: What is the stem of *mīles, mīlitis*?
steps.explain: Take *-is* off the genitive *mīlitis*: *mīlit-*.

answers: rēgem
steps.explain: Stem *rēg-* plus *-em*.

answers: nōmina
steps.explain: A neuter plural: *nōmina*.
*-ī* is the third-declension dative singular. The daughter gives water to her mother.

lessons.title: Urbs, mare, nāvis: i-stems
lessons.summary: Third-declension nouns with an *i* in the genitive plural, and the sea.
objectives: Recognize the i-stem genitive plural *-ium*
Decline *mare*, with its ablative *marī*
Read sentences mixing all three declensions

steps.title: An extra i
body: Some third-declension nouns are **i-stems**. They decline like *rēx*, except that the genitive plural ends in *-ium*, not *-um*.

Two kinds are common: nouns with the same number of syllables in the nominative and genitive (*cīvis, cīvis*; *nāvis, nāvis*), and nouns whose stem ends in two consonants (*urbs, urbis*; *mōns, montis*; *nox, noctis*).

steps.title: Mare
body: Neuter i-stems like *mare* have *-ī* in the ablative singular and *-ia* in the nominative and accusative plural.

steps.explain: *In marī*, with the i-stem ablative *-ī*.

steps.explain: *Rēx, rēgis* has one consonant before the ending and a shorter nominative, so it is not an i-stem: *rēgum*.

lessons.title: Regō, capiō, audiō
lessons.summary: The third and fourth conjugations in the present.

steps.title: Four families
body: Every regular verb belongs to one of four conjugations, and the infinitive shows which: *-āre* (1st), *-ēre* (2nd), *-ere* with a short *e* (3rd), *-īre* (4th).

The third conjugation has a stem ending in a consonant, and a short *i* joins it to most endings. Some third-conjugation verbs, like *capiō*, keep an *i* before some endings: they are called *-iō* verbs.
steps.tip: *Capiō* and *audiō* share *-iō* and *-iunt*. The infinitive tells them apart: *capere* is third, *audīre* fourth.

steps.explain: *-ere* with a short *e*, and a first form in plain *-ō*: third.

lessons.title: Regēbam, regam: past and future
lessons.summary: The imperfect and future of the third and fourth conjugations.
objectives: Form the imperfect with *-ēbā-*
Form the future with *-am, -ēs, -et*
Tell *regis* “you rule” from *regēs* “you will rule”

steps.title: The imperfect: -ēbā-
body: In the third and fourth conjugations the imperfect sign is *-ēbā-*: *regēbam*, *capiēbam*, *audiēbam*. The endings are the ones you know.

examples.en: The king was ruling the city.
The citizens were listening to the voice.

steps.title: The future: -am, -ēs, -et
body: The future of the third and fourth conjugations does not use *-bō*. It uses *-am* for “I”, then *-ē-* with the other endings.
steps.tip: One vowel is all that separates present and future: *regit* “he rules”, *reget* “he will rule”; *regis* “you rule”, *regēs* “you will rule”.

steps.explain: *-et* in the third conjugation is future.
*-it* is the present.

lessons.title: Venī! Commands and calling someone
lessons.summary: The imperative, *nōlī*, and the vocative.
objectives: Give a command to one person or several
Forbid something with *nōlī* and *nōlīte*
Address someone in the vocative

steps.title: Do it!
body: A command to one person is usually just the verb’s stem: *amā!* “love!”, *monē!* “warn!”, *audī!* “listen!”. The third conjugation adds *-e*: *rege!* “rule!”.
To command several people, add *-te* (you met it in *salvēte*). The third conjugation uses *-ite*.
steps.tip: Four common verbs have short singular commands: *dīc!* “say!”, *dūc!* “lead!”, *fac!* “do!”, and *fer!* “carry!”.

steps.title: Don’t!
body: To forbid, use *nōlī* (to one person) or *nōlīte* (to several) with the infinitive. Literally, “be unwilling to…”.

steps.title: Calling someone: the vocative
body: The case for addressing someone is the **vocative**. It is almost always the same as the nominative. The one difference: second-declension nouns in *-us* change to *-e*, and names in *-ius* to *-ī*.

steps.prompt: Type the command “listen!” said to several people.
answers: audīte
steps.explain: *Audī* plus *-te*.

steps.prompt: Type the command “carry!” (from *portō*) said to one person.
answers: portā
steps.explain: The stem: *portā*.

steps.prompt: How do you tell a group of friends not to shout?
steps.explain: Several people: *nōlīte*, with the infinitive *clāmāre*.
*-us* becomes *-e*: *serve*.

units.title: The perfect system
units.blurb: Principal parts, and three tenses built on the perfect stem: *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī*.

lessons.title: Principal parts
lessons.summary: The four forms every Latin verb is learned by.
objectives: Name a verb’s four principal parts
Find the perfect stem from the third principal part
Recognize the regular patterns of the first and fourth conjugations

steps.title: Four forms
body: Until now you have learned verbs by two forms. A dictionary gives four, the **principal parts**: “I love”, “to love”, “I loved”, and the **supine**, a form you will use later.
The third part is the perfect, “I loved”. Take off its *-ī* and you have the **perfect stem**, which three tenses are built on.
steps.tip: First- and fourth-conjugation verbs are nearly all regular: *-āvī, -ātum* and *-īvī, -ītum*. The second and third are less predictable, so learn their parts with the word.

steps.prompt: What is the perfect stem of *dūcō, dūcere, dūxī, ductum*?
steps.explain: Take *-ī* off the third part: *dūx-*.

steps.prompt: What is the perfect stem of *veniō*?
steps.explain: *Vēnī* minus *-ī*: *vēn-*, with a long *ē* that the present does not have.

steps.prompt: Give the third principal part of the regular verb *portō, portāre*.
answers: portāvī
steps.explain: First conjugation: *portāvī*.

steps.prompt: Give the third principal part of the regular verb *dormiō, dormīre*.
answers: dormīvī
steps.explain: Fourth conjugation: *dormīvī*.

steps.prompt: Match each present to its perfect.

steps.explain: *Vincō, vincere, vīcī, victum*: *vīcī* “I conquered”, as in Caesar’s *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī*.

lessons.title: Vēnī, vīdī, vīcī: the perfect
lessons.summary: What happened, once and for all.
objectives: Form the perfect tense of any verb from its perfect stem

steps.title: Perfect endings
body: The perfect has its own set of endings, the same for every verb. Add them to the perfect stem.
steps.tip: The perfect can be “I loved” or “I have loved”. Caesar’s *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī* is “I came, I saw, I conquered”.

steps.explain: Perfect stem *vīd-* and the ending *-ērunt*: “they saw”.

answers: vēnimus

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “he was” in the perfect.

steps.title: Background and event
body: Latin has two main past tenses, and a story uses both. The **imperfect** paints the scene: what was going on, what used to happen. The **perfect** moves the story: what happened next, once.

examples.la: Puerī in agrō ambulā|bant, cum subitō equum vīd|ērunt.
examples.en: The boys were walking in the field when suddenly they saw a horse.
examples.note: The walking is the background; seeing the horse is the event.

examples.la: Saepe ad urbem nāvigā|bat; tum semel ad īnsulam nāvigāv|it.
examples.en: He often used to sail to the city; then, once, he sailed to the island.

steps.tip: Words like *saepe*, *semper* and *cotīdiē* suit the imperfect. *Subitō* and *tum* usually bring a perfect.

steps.prompt: Which fits best? “Suddenly the soldier ___ a voice.”
steps.explain: One sudden event: the perfect *audīvit*.

steps.prompt: Which fits best? “Every day the farmer ___ in the field.”
steps.explain: A repeated habit: the imperfect *labōrābat*.

steps.prompt: In this sentence, which verb is the background?
steps.explain: The sailors were sleeping (imperfect, the scene) when the storm came (perfect, the event). *Cum* here means “when”.

steps.latin: Puella in viā stābat; tum amīcum vīdit.
answers: The girl was standing in the road; then she saw her friend.
The girl was standing in the street; then she saw a friend.
The girl stood in the road; then she saw her friend.

steps.latin: Rōmānī saepe pugnābant, sed hodiē nōn pugnāvērunt.

lessons.title: Had done, will have done

steps.title: The pluperfect: had done
body: The **pluperfect** says what had already happened before another past event. Build it from the perfect stem and the endings of *eram*.

steps.title: The future perfect: will have done
body: The **future perfect** says what will already have happened by some point in the future. It uses the perfect stem and endings like *erō*, except that “they” is *-erint*.
Latin uses it more strictly than English: “When you come, I will tell you” is, in Latin, “When you will have come”: *Cum vēneris, tibi dīcam*.

steps.explain: Perfect stem *vēn-* plus *-erant*: pluperfect, “they had come”.
*-erit* on the perfect stem is the future perfect.

lessons.title: Ego, tū, nōs, vōs

objectives: Decline *ego*, *tū*, *nōs* and *vōs*

steps.title: Me and you
body: Latin needs no word for “I” as a subject, since the verb says it. So *ego* and *tū* in the nominative are for emphasis: *Ego poēta sum, tū nauta es*, “*I* am a poet; *you* are a sailor”.
The other cases are used all the time.
steps.tip: *Cum* is joined to the end of these: *mēcum* “with me”, *tēcum* “with you”, *nōbīscum*, *vōbīscum*.

steps.title: My, your, our
body: The possessives are adjectives, and agree with the thing possessed, not the owner: a woman says *pater meus*, “my father”, because *pater* is masculine.

steps.explain: *Mihi* is the dative: my friend gives a gift to me.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “with you” (one person).

lessons.title: Is, ea, id; suus
lessons.summary: “He, she, it, they”, and the difference between *eius* and *suus*.
objectives: Decline *is, ea, id*
Translate *eius* and *eōrum* as “his, her, their”
Tell *suus* (his own) from *eius* (someone else’s)

words.english: his own, her own, their own

steps.title: He, she, it
body: *Is, ea, id* points back to someone or something already mentioned: “he”, “she”, “it”, “they”. It can also stand with a noun: *is puer*, “that boy”.

steps.title: Gender follows the thing, not the English
body: The pronoun takes the gender of the noun it stands for. A city is feminine, so “it” for *urbs* is *ea*; a sword is masculine, so “it” for *gladius* is *is*.

examples.en: I see Marcus; I love him.
We saw the city; it was large.

steps.title: His own, or someone else’s
body: English “his” is ambiguous; Latin is not. **Suus** means the subject’s own: *his own, her own, their own*. **Eius** (and *eōrum*, *eārum*) means someone else’s.

examples.en: Marcus loves his horse, someone else’s.

steps.tip: *Suus* is an adjective, so it agrees with the thing owned (*equum suum*). *Eius* is a genitive, so it never changes for the thing owned.

steps.latin: Puellam vocāvī, sed eam nōn vīdī.
steps.explain: *Eam* is feminine accusative singular, pointing back to *puellam*.
*Suum*: the subject’s own.
*Eius*: someone else’s son, a man already mentioned.

steps.prompt: Type the dative singular of *is*, “to him”.
answers: eī
steps.explain: *Eī*.

steps.prompt: Type the accusative plural feminine of *is*, “them” (women).
answers: eās
steps.explain: *Eās*.

answers: The soldiers came; the king praised them.

lessons.title: Hic and ille
lessons.summary: “This” and “that”, and how they turn into “the latter” and “the former”.
objectives: Decline *hic, haec, hoc* and *ille, illa, illud*

steps.title: This and that
body: *Hic* points to something near the speaker, “this”; *ille* to something farther off, “that”. Both work as adjectives (*hic puer*, “this boy”) or on their own (*hic*, “this man”, “he”).
Both have a genitive singular in *-ius* and a dative in *-ī* for every gender, like *is*.

steps.title: The plural
body: In the plural, *ille* declines like *bonus*; *hic* is a little irregular.
steps.tip: Paired in one sentence, *hic … ille* means “the latter … the former”: *hic* is the one mentioned last, nearer in the text.

steps.explain: *Urbs* is feminine: *haec urbs*, “this city”.
*Mīlitem* is masculine accusative singular: *illum mīlitem*, “that soldier”.

answers: huic
steps.explain: *Huic puellae*.

This boy is good, that boy is bad.

lessons.title: Quī, quae, quod
lessons.summary: Who, which, that: joining two sentences with the relative pronoun.
objectives: Decline the relative pronoun

steps.title: Who, which, that
body: A **relative pronoun** begins a clause that describes a noun, its **antecedent**: “the girl *whom you see*”, “the gift *which you sent*”.
Here is the rule that makes relatives easy: the relative takes its **gender and number** from the antecedent, but its **case** from its job in its own clause.

steps.title: Gender from outside, case from inside
body: In *Puella quam vidēs soror mea est*, “The girl whom you see is my sister”, *quam* is feminine singular because of *puella*, but accusative because it is the object of *vidēs*.

examples.la: Puella qu|am vidēs soror mea est.
examples.en: The girl whom you see is my sister.

examples.la: Mīles qu|ī urbem servāvit fīdus erat.
examples.en: The soldier who saved the city was loyal.
The gift which you sent is beautiful.

examples.la: Hominēs qu|ibus aquam dedimus laetī sunt.
examples.en: The people to whom we gave water are happy.

steps.explain: *Quem* is masculine singular, pointing back to *amīcus*: the friend whom I called is not coming.

options: The relative is the object of *vīdimus* in its own clause
steps.explain: Feminine singular from *urbs*, but accusative because we saw it: *quam*.
The citizens love him: object, so accusative *quem*, masculine for *rēx*.

lines.la: Subitō ūvās vīdit, quae in altā vīte pendēbant.

lines.la: “Hae ūvae,” inquit, “mihi erunt!”

lines.la: Saluit, sed eās nōn tetigit.

She is talking about different grapes

objectives: Decline third-declension adjectives of one, two and three endings

steps.title: A third kind of adjective
body: Some adjectives use third-declension endings. Most have two forms in the nominative: one for masculine and feminine, one for neuter: *fortis, forte*. A few have one for all three (*ingēns*), and a few have three (*ācer, ācris, ācre*).
They are i-stems: ablative singular in *-ī*, genitive plural in *-ium*, neuter plural in *-ia*.
steps.tip: Agreement is in gender, number and case, not declension. *Puella fortis*, *nauta fortis* and *mīles fortis* are all right.

steps.explain: *Nautae* is masculine nominative plural: *fortēs*.
*Dōna* is neuter plural: *omnia*.

lessons.summary: The fourth and fifth declensions, and the special forms of *domus*.
objectives: Decline fourth-declension nouns like *manus*

steps.title: The fourth declension
body: Fourth-declension nouns have a genitive in *-ūs*. Most are masculine, like *exercitus*; *manus* and *domus* are feminine.
steps.tip: Only the macron tells *manus*, “hand” (nominative), from *manūs*, “of the hand” or “hands”.

steps.title: The fifth declension
body: The fifth declension is small but important: *rēs*, *diēs*, *spēs*, *fidēs*. Its genitive ends in *-eī* (or *-ēī*).
*Rēs* is Latin’s most flexible noun: thing, matter, affair, event, situation. *Rēs pūblica* is “the public thing”: the state, the republic.

steps.title: At home, homeward, from home
body: *Domus* uses special forms, with no preposition: *domī* “at home”, *domum* “home, homeward”, *domō* “from home”.

steps.explain: The genitive *-ūs* marks the fourth declension. (A second-declension noun would have *-ī*.)

lessons.title: Amor: the passive voice
lessons.summary: Is loved, was being loved, will be loved; and who did it, *ā* or *ab*.
objectives: Form the present, imperfect and future passive

Tell the agent (a person) from the means (a thing)

steps.title: Active and passive
body: In the **active** voice the subject does the action: “The sailor loves the girl.” In the **passive** the subject has it done to them: “The girl is loved by the sailor.”
Latin makes the passive by changing the personal endings: *-r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur*.

steps.title: Past and future
body: The imperfect and future change the same way. Keep the tense sign and swap in the passive ending: *amābat* → *amābātur*, “he was being loved”; *amābit* → *amābitur*, “he will be loved”; *reget* → *regētur*, “he will be ruled”.
The first-person forms are *-bar* and *-bor* (*amābar*, *amābor*), and in the third and fourth conjugations *-ar* (*regar*, “I will be ruled”).

examples.en: We were being called by the king.

steps.title: By whom, by what
body: The person who does a passive action goes in the ablative with *ā* or *ab*: this is the **ablative of agent**. A thing that does it is a plain ablative of means, with no preposition.

examples.en: The city is being captured by the soldiers.
The city is being captured with swords.

Because the participle is an adjective, it agrees with the subject in gender, number and case: *puer vocātus est*, *puella vocāta est*, *dōnum missum est*.

units.blurb: Verbs that look passive but mean active, and the everyday verbs that go their own way: *possum*, *volō*, *eō*, *ferō*, *fīō*.

lessons.title: Loquor: deponent verbs
lessons.summary: Verbs that are passive in form and active in meaning.
objectives: Recognize a deponent verb from its dictionary entry
Translate deponent forms actively, in every tense
Give a deponent’s infinitive and imperative

steps.title: Passive in form, active in meaning
body: Some Latin verbs have only passive forms, but they are translated actively. *Hortātur* looks like “he is encouraged”, yet it means “he encourages”. These are **deponent** verbs, from *dēpōnō*, “I lay aside”: they have laid aside their active forms.
You can spot one in the dictionary. It has three principal parts, not four, and all three are passive: *hortor, hortārī, hortātus sum*.
steps.tip: The infinitive gives it away too. A deponent’s infinitive is passive in form: *hortārī*, “to encourage”; *loquī*, “to speak”.

steps.title: Every tense, every conjugation
body: Deponents come in all four conjugations and use every passive form you learned in Level I: *hortābātur*, “he was encouraging”; *sequētur*, “he will follow”; *proficīscēmur*, “we will set out”.
The perfect is the participle with *sum*, and the participle agrees with the subject, just as in the passive: *puella locūta est*, “the girl spoke”.
The imperative is the one surprise. The singular looks like an active infinitive, and the plural like a passive “you (all)”: *sequere!* “follow!”, *sequiminī!* “follow, all of you!”

examples.en: The slave was following his master.
The girl spoke for a long time.

steps.explain: A deponent: passive ending, active meaning. “He encourages.”

lessons.title: Morior, patior, ūtor
lessons.summary: More deponents, the ablative with *ūtor*, and verbs that are only half deponent.

steps.title: Deponents like capiō
body: A deponent follows the conjugation of its stem. *Morior*, *patior* and *ēgredior* are third-conjugation *-iō* verbs, so they go like the passive of *capiō*: *capior, caperis, capitur*.
steps.tip: *Patior* also means “allow”, with an infinitive: *nōn patitur puerōs abīre*, “he does not allow the boys to leave”.

steps.title: Ūtor and the ablative
body: A few deponents take their object in the ablative, not the accusative. The most common is *ūtor*, “I use”: literally something like “I help myself by means of”, which is why the ablative makes sense.

examples.en: The sailors used a large ship.

steps.tip: Students remember the five as PUFFV: *potior* “take possession of”, *ūtor* “use”, *fruor* “enjoy”, *fungor* “perform”, *vēscor* “feed on”. All take the ablative.

steps.title: Half deponent
body: A few verbs are **semi-deponent**: active in the present, imperfect and future, deponent in the perfect. *Audeō, audēre, ausus sum*: *audet* is “he dares”, and *ausus est* is “he dared”.
Likewise *gaudeō, gaudēre, gāvīsus sum*, “to rejoice”, and *soleō, solēre, solitus sum*, “to be used to”.

examples.en: The boy does not dare to walk into the forest.

*Audeō* is semi-deponent: its perfect *ausa est* is active, “she dared”.

lessons.title: Possum: I can
lessons.summary: *Possum*, and the infinitive that finishes its meaning.
objectives: Conjugate *possum* in the present, imperfect, future and perfect

steps.title: Pot- and sum
body: *Possum* is *pot-*, “able”, joined to *sum*. Where the form of *sum* begins with *s*, *pot-* becomes *pos-*: *possum*, but *potest*.
Every tense follows *sum*: imperfect *poteram*, “I was able, I could”; future *poterō*, “I will be able”. The perfect is regular from *potuī*: *potuit*, “he was able”.

steps.title: Can what?
body: *Possum* rarely stands alone: an infinitive finishes its meaning. *Nāvigāre possum*, “I can sail”. This is the **complementary infinitive**.
Many verbs take one: *dēbeō*, “I ought (to)”; *cupiō*, “I want (to)”; *incipiō*, “I begin (to)”; *audeō*, “I dare (to)”; *soleō*, “I usually”.
A present infinitive is the second principal part: *amāre, monēre, regere, audīre*, and for a deponent *hortārī, loquī*.

steps.title: Three irregular presents
body: *Nōlō* is *nōn* + *volō*, and *mālō* is *magis*, “more”, + *volō*: “I want more”, that is, “I prefer”. Their presents are irregular and have to be learned by heart.
steps.tip: You already know *nōlī*: it is the imperative of *nōlō*. *Nōlī timēre* is literally “be unwilling to fear”, that is, “don’t be afraid”.

steps.title: The other tenses are regular
body: Only the present is odd. The imperfect and future go like *regō*: *volēbam*, “I wanted”; *volam, volēs, volet*, “I will want”. So *nōlēbam*, *nōlam*, *mālēbam*, *mālam*. The perfect is regular from the third principal part: *voluī, nōluī, māluī*.
All three take a complementary infinitive, and *mālō* often has *quam*, “than”.

examples.en: I would rather sail than walk.

steps.tip: Watch for *volō, volāre*, “to fly”, a regular first-conjugation verb: *volat*, “it flies”. *Vult* can only be “wants”.

lessons.title: Eō and ferō
lessons.summary: Go and carry: two short verbs with a great many compounds.
objectives: Conjugate *eō* and *ferō* in the present

steps.title: Eō, I go
body: *Eō* is built on the stem *i-*, which becomes *e-* before *a*, *o* or *u*: *eō, īs, it, īmus, ītis, eunt*. The imperfect is *ībam* and the future *ībō*, like a first-conjugation verb. The perfect is *iī* (or *īvī*).
Prefixes make its compounds, which conjugate the same way: *abeō* “go away”, *adeō* “go to”, *exeō* “go out”, *redeō* “go back”, *trānseō* “go across”, and *pereō*, “go through”, that is, “perish”.

steps.title: Ferō, I carry
body: *Ferō* goes like *regō*, except that a few forms drop the vowel: *fers, fert, fertis*, and the infinitive *ferre*. Its principal parts come from two different roots: *ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum*.
Its compounds are all over English: *trānsferō* (transfer), *referō* (refer), *cōnferō* (confer), *offerō* (offer).
steps.tip: *Rettulī*, the perfect of *referō*, has a double *t*: *re-* + *tulī*.

steps.explain: *Eunt*, “they go”: the stem *i-* becomes *e-* before *u*.

steps.title: The reverse of a deponent
body: *Faciō* has no ordinary present passive. Latin uses *fīō* instead, which is active in form but passive in meaning, the reverse of a deponent: *fit*, “it is done, it happens”; *fīunt*, “they become”.
Its perfect is simply the perfect passive of *faciō*: *factus est*, “he became” or “it was done”. The infinitive is *fierī*.

lessons.title: Captus: the perfect participle
lessons.summary: A verb used as an adjective: *urbs capta*, “the captured city”.
objectives: Form the perfect passive participle from the fourth principal part
Make it agree with its noun
Translate it with “having been”, or as a clause

steps.title: A verb as an adjective
body: In the perfect passive, *urbs capta est*, you met the **perfect passive participle**: the fourth principal part, declined like *bonus, -a, -um*. It can also stand on its own as an adjective, agreeing with a noun in gender, number and case.
Literally it means “having been …ed”, and it describes something that happened **before** the main verb.

examples.en: The soldiers left the captured city.

steps.title: Better English
body: “Having been defeated” is clumsy English. A participle often reads best as a clause: “the enemy, **who had been** defeated, fled”; “**when** they had been defeated, the enemy fled”; “**after** they were defeated…”. Choose what the sense needs.
Latin uses participles far more than English does. A long sentence in Caesar or Vergil often turns on two or three of them.

steps.title: The -ns participle
body: The **present active participle** ends in *-ns* and means “…ing”: *vocāns*, “calling”. It is made from the present stem.
It is a third-declension adjective with one form for all genders in the nominative, like *ingēns*. The genitive shows the stem: *vocāns, vocantis*.
steps.tip: In the ablative singular a participle usually ends in *-e*, *vocante*, not the *-ī* of adjectives like *ingentī*.

steps.title: At the same time
body: A present participle shows an action going on **at the same time** as the main verb, whatever tense that is. English often uses “while” or “as”.
Deponents have present participles too, and they are active like the rest of the verb: *loquēns*, “speaking”; *moriēns*, “dying”.

steps.title: About to
body: The **future active participle** is the fourth principal part with *-ūrus, -ūra, -ūrum* in place of *-us*: *vocātūrus*, “about to call”; *captūrus*, “about to capture”. It is declined like *bonus*.
Two are worth knowing on their own: *futūrus*, “about to be”, from *sum*, which gives English “future”; and *moritūrus*, “about to die”, from *morior*.

As he was about to leave, the sailor said “goodbye” to his daughter.

steps.title: Three participles, three times
body: Each participle is timed against the main verb: the present is the **same time**, the perfect is **before**, the future is **after**.
Only the perfect is passive. The other two are active, and a deponent’s perfect participle is active as well.

lessons.title: Urbe captā: the ablative absolute
lessons.summary: A noun and a participle in the ablative, standing apart from the rest of the sentence.
objectives: Recognize an ablative absolute
Translate it with “when”, “after”, “since” or “although”
Recognize the kind with no participle: *Caesare duce*

words.english: consul, one of the two chief magistrates of Rome

steps.title: Absolute: set free
body: A noun and a participle, both in the ablative, can stand apart from the rest of the sentence and give its circumstances. This is the **ablative absolute**. *Absolūtus* means “set free”: the phrase is not tied grammatically to any other word.
Literally it is “the city having been captured”. In good English, choose the conjunction the sense needs: **when**, **after**, **since**, **although**.

examples.en: When the city had been captured, the soldiers left.
After the signal was given, the soldiers began to fight.
As the enemy came on, the citizens were afraid.

steps.tip: An ablative absolute is usually set off by commas, and its noun is never the subject or object of the main verb.

steps.title: Without a participle
body: *Sum* has no present participle, so Latin simply puts two nouns, or a noun and an adjective, in the ablative: *Caesare duce*, “with Caesar as leader, under Caesar’s command”; *Cicerōne cōnsule*, “when Cicero was consul”.
Romans named years this way, by their two consuls: *Pompeiō et Crassō cōnsulibus*, “in the consulship of Pompey and Crassus”, that is, 55 BC.

examples.en: Under Caesar’s command, the Romans conquered Gaul.

lessons.title: Reading: Horātius Cocles

steps.title: Horātius Cocles
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 2. About 508 BC: the Etruscan king Porsenna marches on Rome, and only the Tiber and one wooden bridge stand in his way.

lines.la: Porsenna, rēx Etrūscōrum, cum magnō exercitū ad urbem Rōmam vēnit.
lines.en: Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, came to the city of Rome with a large army.

lines.la: Rōmānī, hostibus vīsīs, ex agrīs in urbem fūgērunt.
lines.en: When they saw the enemy, the Romans fled from the fields into the city.

lines.la: Ūnus pōns, Sublicius nōmine, iter hostibus dabat.
lines.en: One bridge, called the Sublician, gave the enemy a way in.

lines.la: Tum Horātius Cocles, fortis mīles, ad pontem cucurrit et cīvēs fugientēs hortātus est:
lines.en: Then Horatius Cocles, a brave soldier, ran to the bridge and urged on the fleeing citizens:

lines.la: “Pontem post mē frangite! Ego hostēs sustinēbō.”
lines.en: “Break down the bridge behind me! I will hold off the enemy.”

lines.la: Sōlus in prīmā parte pontis stetit, hostibus impetum facientibus.

lines.la: Etrūscī, virtūtem eius mīrantēs, diū prōgredī nōn audēbant.

lines.la: Deinde armātus in flūmen dēsiluit et ad suōs incolumis trānāvit.
lines.en: Then, still armed, he leapt down into the river and swam across to his own people unharmed.

lines.la: Rōmānī, virō servātō, gāvīsī sunt, et statua eius in forō posita est.
lines.en: The Romans rejoiced that the man had been saved, and a statue of him was set up in the Forum.

lessons.title: Six infinitives
lessons.summary: To love, to be loved, to have loved: every infinitive, active and passive.
objectives: Form the present, perfect and future infinitives, active and passive
Recognize an infinitive’s tense and voice at sight

steps.title: Tense and voice
body: You know the present infinitive, *amāre*, “to love”. Latin has six in all: present, perfect and future, each active and passive.
The present passive changes *-re* to *-rī*: *amārī*, “to be loved”; *monērī*; *audīrī*. The third conjugation has just *-ī*: *regī*, *capī*.
The perfect active adds *-isse* to the perfect stem: *amāvisse*, “to have loved”; *vīdisse*, “to have seen”. The perfect passive is the participle with *esse*: *amātus esse*, “to have been loved”.
The future active is the future participle with *esse*: *amātūrus esse*, “to be about to love”. The future passive, *amātum īrī*, is rare.

rows.label: Perfect
cells: amātus esse, to have been loved

rows.label: Future
cells: amātūrus esse, to be about to love
amātum īrī, to be about to be loved

steps.tip: A deponent has three: *hortārī*, “to encourage”; *hortātus esse*, “to have encouraged”; *hortātūrus esse*, “to be about to encourage”.

options: perfect passive: to have been seen
steps.explain: The perfect stem *vīd-* + *-isse*.
*-rī* in place of *-re*: “to be heard”.
The perfect passive participle with *esse*.

answers: vocāvisse

steps.prompt: Type the present passive infinitive of *regō*.
answers: regī
steps.explain: In the third conjugation the present passive infinitive is plain *-ī*: *regī*, “to be ruled”.

steps.prompt: Type the present passive infinitive of *moneō*.
answers: monērī
steps.explain: *Monēre* → *monērī*, “to be warned”.

steps.explain: *Ventūrus*, “about to come”, with *esse*.

lessons.title: Dīcit eum venīre
lessons.summary: Reporting what someone says or thinks: the accusative and infinitive.
objectives: Recognize the verbs that introduce indirect statement
Translate the accusative and infinitive with “that”

steps.title: He says that…
body: English reports speech with “that”: “He says **that** his father is coming.” Latin has no word for this “that”. It puts the subject of the reported statement in the **accusative** and its verb in the **infinitive**: *Dīcit patrem venīre*, literally “He says father to be coming”.
This is **indirect statement**. It follows verbs of saying, thinking, knowing and perceiving: *dīcō, nūntiō, putō, crēdō, sciō, sentiō, intellegō, spērō, videō, audiō*.

examples.en: The boy says that his father is coming.
The sailors think that land is near.
We know that Rome is great.

steps.tip: When you meet a verb of saying or thinking, look ahead for an accusative and an infinitive, and supply “that”.

steps.title: Everything follows the accusative
body: In the reported statement, adjectives and participles that describe the subject agree with it, so they are accusative too: *Putō puellās laetās esse*, “I think that the girls are happy.”

options: Marcus says that his friend is coming.
Marcus tells his friend to come.
Marcus’s friend says that he is coming.
steps.explain: An accusative, *amīcum*, and an infinitive, *venīre*, after *dīcit*.

lessons.title: Before, during, after
lessons.summary: The tense of the infinitive, and translating when the main verb is past.
objectives: Use the present, perfect and future infinitives for same time, before and after

steps.title: Time is relative
body: The infinitive’s tense is **relative** to the main verb: present is the same time, perfect is before, future is after.
With a present main verb, English follows naturally. With a past main verb, English shifts every tense back a step: “he says they **are** coming” becomes “he said they **were** coming”.
steps.tip: In a compound infinitive the participle agrees with the accusative subject: *mīlitēs ventūrōs esse*, *urbem captam esse*.

steps.title: Reports and news
body: Most of the indirect statements you will read report news or thoughts about the past. Read the infinitive, decide its time, then choose the English tense.

examples.en: He reported that the city had been captured.
We learned that the king had died.
He promised that his father would come.

options: He said that the enemy were fleeing.

options: They thought that the king was coming.

steps.explain: A future infinitive after a past verb: “would come”.

options: They reported that the ship was in the harbor.

They reported that the ship would be in the harbor.
steps.explain: A present infinitive: the same time as *nūntiāvērunt*, so “was”.

lessons.title: Sē, negō, and dīcitur
lessons.summary: Who is “he”? The reflexive in reported speech, *negō*, and “he is said to”.
objectives: Use *sē* and *suus* for the speaker, *eum* and *eius* for someone else
Translate *negō* as “say that … not”
Translate *dīcitur* and *vidētur* with an infinitive

words.english: to found, establish; to hide, bury

steps.title: Himself or someone else?
body: Inside an indirect statement, *sē* and *suus* point back to the subject of the verb of saying. *Eum* and *eius* point to someone else.
The reflexive pronoun *sē* has no nominative: accusative *sē*, genitive *suī*, dative *sibi*, ablative *sē*, the same in the singular and the plural.

examples.en: Marcus says that he (Marcus) is happy.
Marcus says that he (someone else) is happy.

examples.la: Puellae putant sē patrem suum vīsūrās esse.
examples.en: The girls think that they will see their father.

steps.title: Negō, iubeō, dīcitur
body: Latin prefers *negō* to *dīcō … nōn*: *Negat sē timēre*, “He says that he is not afraid.”
*Iubeō*, “order”, also takes an accusative and an infinitive: *Rēx mīlitēs pugnāre iussit*, “The king ordered the soldiers to fight.”

In the passive, *dīcitur* and *vidētur* keep their subject in the nominative: *Rōmulus urbem condidisse dīcitur*, “Romulus is said to have founded the city”; *Puella laeta esse vidētur*, “The girl seems to be happy.”
steps.tip: With an infinitive, *vidētur* is “seems”, not “is seen”.

steps.explain: *Sē* refers to the subject of *dīcit*: Julia herself.
*Eum*, not *sē*: someone other than Marcus.

options: He said that he was not afraid.

options: Romulus says that he founded the city.

It is said that the city founded Romulus.
steps.explain: *Dīcitur* with a nominative subject and an infinitive: “is said to have founded”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “The king ordered the soldiers to fight.”

steps.explain: *Iubeō* takes an accusative and an infinitive: *mīlitēs pugnāre*.

steps.title: Mūcius Scaevola
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 2. Horatius has saved the bridge, but Porsenna’s army still surrounds Rome.

lines.la: Porsenna, urbe obsessā, Rōmam capere cōnābātur.
lines.en: Porsenna had besieged the city and was trying to take Rome.

lines.la: Gāius Mūcius, iuvenis nōbilis, rēgem interficere cōnstituit.
lines.en: Gaius Mucius, a young nobleman, decided to kill the king.

lines.la: In castra hostium intrāvit, sed errāns scrībam rēgis prō rēge interfēcit.
lines.en: He got into the enemy camp, but by mistake killed the king’s secretary instead of the king.

lines.la: Ā mīlitibus captus ad rēgem ductus est.
lines.en: He was captured by the soldiers and brought to the king.

lines.la: “Rōmānus sum,” inquit, “et sciō multōs aliōs iuvenēs idem facere velle.”

lessons.title: Altior: the comparative
lessons.summary: More, rather, too: *-ior*, and two ways to say “than”.
objectives: Form and decline the comparative adjective

steps.title: More, rather, too
body: The **comparative** adds *-ior* (masculine and feminine) or *-ius* (neuter) to the adjective’s stem, which you find from the genitive: *altus, altī* → *altior, altius*, “higher”; *fēlīx, fēlīcis* → *fēlīcior*, “luckier”; *celer, celeris* → *celerior*, “quicker”.
It means “more …”, but also “rather …” or “too …” when nothing is being compared: *via longior* can be “a rather long road”.
The comparative is a third-declension adjective but not an i-stem: ablative *-e*, genitive plural *-um*, neuter plural *-a*.

steps.title: Than
body: “Than” is *quam*, and the two things compared are in the same case: *Mōns altior est quam urbs*, “The mountain is higher than the city.”
Or Latin leaves out *quam* and puts the second thing in the ablative: the **ablative of comparison**. *Mōns urbe altior est* means the same.

examples.en: A ship is faster than a horse.
The boy is taller than his father.

steps.explain: *-ior* is the comparative: “longer”.
Feminine nominative, agreeing with *via*: *longior*. *Longius* is neuter.

options: Our ship is as fast as yours.
Our ship is faster than yours.

options: an ablative of comparison: “than the city”
an ablative of place: “in the city”
an ablative of means: “by the city”
steps.explain: With a comparative and no *quam*, the ablative means “than”.

The boy is taller than the father.

lessons.title: Optimus: the superlative
lessons.summary: Most, very: *-issimus*, and the adjectives that compare irregularly.
objectives: Form the superlative, including *-errimus* and *-illimus*

Translate *quam* with a superlative

steps.title: Most, very
body: The **superlative** adds *-issimus, -a, -um* to the stem: *altissimus*, “highest”; *fēlīcissimus*, “luckiest”. It means “most …” or just “very …”: *mōns altissimus*, “a very high mountain”.
Adjectives ending in *-er* add *-rimus* to the nominative: *pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*; *ācer* → *ācerrimus*; *miser* → *miserrimus*.
Six adjectives in *-lis* take *-limus*: *facilis* → *facillimus*, and so *difficilis, similis, dissimilis, gracilis* “slender”, *humilis* “low”.
steps.tip: *Quam* with a superlative means “as … as possible”: *quam celerrimus*, “as fast as possible”.

steps.title: Good, better, best
body: The commonest adjectives compare irregularly, as they do in English, and English has borrowed most of them: ameliorate, optimist, pejorative, pessimist, major, maximum, minor, minimum, plural.

steps.explain: The superlative: “highest” or “very high”.
An *-er* adjective: *pulcher* + *-rimus*.

*Malus, peior, pessimus*: bad, worse, worst.

lessons.title: Fortiter: adverbs
lessons.summary: How something is done: *-ē* and *-iter*, and comparing adverbs.
objectives: Make adverbs from adjectives of every declension
Form comparative and superlative adverbs, including *bene, melius, optimē*

steps.title: Making an adverb
body: Adjectives of the first and second declensions make adverbs with *-ē*: *lātus* → *lātē*, “widely”; *miser* → *miserē*, “wretchedly”; *līber* → *līberē*, “freely”.

Third-declension adjectives use *-iter*: *fortis* → *fortiter*, “bravely”; *ācer* → *ācriter*, “fiercely”; *celer* → *celeriter*, “quickly”. Those in *-ns* use *-nter*: *sapiēns* → *sapienter*, “wisely”.
steps.tip: Some adverbs are simply a case form: *facile*, “easily”; *multum*, “much”; *prīmum*, “first”.

steps.title: Comparing adverbs
body: The comparative adverb is the neuter comparative adjective: *fortius*, “more bravely”. The superlative ends in *-ē*: *fortissimē*, “most bravely, very bravely”.
The irregular ones follow their adjectives: *bene, melius, optimē*; *male, peius, pessimē*; *magnopere, magis, maximē*; *multum, plūs, plūrimum*; *parum, minus, minimē*.

examples.en: The soldiers fought as bravely as possible.

steps.explain: A third-declension adjective plus *-iter*: “bravely”.
A first/second-declension adjective takes *-ē*: *miserē*.
*Bene, melius, optimē*: the girl sings better than the boy.

lessons.title: Ūnus, duo, trēs
lessons.summary: Counting to a thousand, first to tenth, and the nine adjectives that go like *ūnus*.
objectives: Count to ten, and know *centum* and *mīlle*
Decline *ūnus*, *duo* and *trēs*, and use *mīlia* with the genitive
Read Roman numerals
Recognize the genitive *-īus* and dative *-ī* of *tōtus*, *nūllus* and the rest

steps.title: Counting
body: Most numbers never change their form: *quattuor* 4, *quīnque* 5, *sex* 6, *septem* 7, *octō* 8, *novem* 9, *decem* 10, and *centum* 100. Only *ūnus*, *duo*, *trēs* and the plural *mīlia* decline.
The ordinals, “first, second …”, are ordinary adjectives like *bonus*: *prīmus, secundus, tertius, quārtus, quīntus, sextus, septimus, octāvus, nōnus, decimus*.
Roman numerals: I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500, M 1000. A smaller numeral before a larger one is subtracted: IV 4, IX 9, XC 90.
steps.tip: *Trēs* goes like a third-declension plural: *trēs* (neuter *tria*), *trium*, *tribus*.

steps.title: Mīlle and mīlia
body: *Mīlle*, “a thousand”, is an adjective that never changes: *mīlle mīlitēs*, “a thousand soldiers”. Its plural *mīlia* is a neuter noun, and what is counted goes in the genitive: *tria mīlia mīlitum*, “three thousand soldiers”, literally “three thousands of soldiers”.

steps.title: Ūnus, and eight like it
body: *Ūnus* has a genitive singular in *-īus* and a dative in *-ī*, in every gender: *ūnīus*, *ūnī*. Eight common adjectives do the same. Students remember all nine as UNUS NAUTA: *ūllus* “any”, *nūllus* “no”, *uter* “which of two”, *sōlus* “alone”, *neuter* “neither”, *alius* “other”, *ūnus* “one”, *tōtus* “whole”, *alter* “the other of two”.
In every other case they go like *bonus*: *tōtam urbem*, “the whole city”; *nūllō modō*, “in no way”.

examples.en: He was the leader of the whole city.

steps.explain: Feminine nominative: *duae puellae*.

lessons.title: Ipse, īdem, quis
lessons.summary: Himself, the same, and asking “who?”
objectives: Tell emphatic *ipse* from reflexive *sē*
Decline *īdem*
Ask questions with *quis* and *quid*

words.english: himself, herself, itself (for emphasis); the very

steps.title: Ipse: emphasis
body: *Ipse* adds emphasis, like “himself” in “the king himself came”: *Rēx ipse vēnit*. It is not reflexive. *Sē* is “himself” as an object; *ipse* is “himself” for emphasis.
It declines like *ille*, with genitive *ipsīus* and dative *ipsī*, and agrees with its noun: *ipsa urbs*, “the city itself”; *eō ipsō diē*, “on that very day”.

steps.title: Īdem: the same
body: *Īdem* is *is, ea, id* with *-dem* added: “that very one”, so “the same”. A few forms change for the sound: *eundem*, *eandem*, and in the plural *eōrundem*.
steps.tip: The nominative plural is *eīdem* (or *īdem*), *eaedem*, *eadem*.

steps.title: Quis? Quid?
body: The interrogative pronoun asks “who?” or “what?”: *quis?* and *quid?* Apart from those, it has the forms of the relative *quī, quae, quod*: *cuius?* “whose?”, *cui?* “to whom?”, *quem?* “whom?”, *quō?* “by whom?”
Before a noun, Latin uses the interrogative adjective, which looks just like the relative: *Quae puella?* “Which girl?” *Quod dōnum?* “Which gift?”

examples.en: To whom did you give the gift?

steps.tip: *Alius … alius* is “one … another”, and *alter … alter* “the one … the other” of two.

lessons.title: Reading: Horātiī et Cūriātiī
lessons.summary: Three brothers against three, and one clever retreat. From Livy.
objectives: Read a story told in numbers and comparisons
Recognize superlative adverbs and forms of *īdem* in context

steps.title: Horātiī et Cūriātiī
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 1. Rome and its mother city, Alba Longa, are at war, and the kings agree to settle it without a battle.

lines.la: Rōmānī et Albānī bellum gerēbant, sed rēgēs magnam caedem timēbant.
lines.en: The Romans and the Albans were at war, but the kings feared a great slaughter.

lines.la: In utrōque exercitū erant trēs frātrēs, eādem aetāte et eīsdem vīribus.
lines.en: In each army there were three brothers, of the same age and the same strength.

lines.la: Rōmānī Horātiī, Albānī Cūriātiī appellābantur.
lines.en: The Romans were called the Horatii, the Albans the Curiatii.

lines.la: Signō datō, sex iuvenēs ācerrimē pugnāre incēpērunt.
lines.en: When the signal was given, the six young men began to fight very fiercely.

lines.la: Mox duo Rōmānī mortuī cecidērunt; trēs Albānī vulnerātī sunt.
lines.en: Soon two of the Romans fell dead; all three Albans were wounded.

lines.la: Tertius Horātius integer erat, sed sōlus contrā trēs; itaque fugere simulāvit.
lines.en: The third Horatius was unhurt, but alone against three; so he pretended to run away.

lines.la: Cūriātiī eum secūtī sunt, alius celerius, alius tardius, quod vulnera eōrum dissimilia erant.
lines.en: The Curiatii followed him, one faster, another more slowly, because their wounds were not alike.

lines.la: Horātius, ad prīmum conversus, eum facillimē interfēcit, deinde secundum, deinde tertium.
lines.en: Horatius turned to face the first and killed him very easily, then the second, then the third.

lines.la: Ita ūnus Rōmānus trēs Albānōs vīcit, et Rōma Albae imperāvit.
lines.en: So one Roman defeated three Albans, and Rome ruled over Alba.

gloss.meaning: to wage war, be at war
